# Proof

We verify that $\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{\infty} \frac{e^{-j}\,j^{j-1}}{j!}=1$.

## Step 1. A generating function

Define
$$
T(x)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{n^{\,n-1}}{n!}\,x^{n}.
$$
By Cayley's formula ($n^{n-2}$ labeled trees on $n$ vertices, hence $n^{n-1}$ rooted labeled trees), $T(x)$ is the exponential generating function of rooted labeled trees. It satisfies the functional equation
$$
T(x)=x\,e^{T(x)}. \tag{1}
$$

This is confirmed by Lagrange inversion. Writing (1) as $T=x\,\varphi(T)$ with $\varphi(u)=e^{u}$, Lagrange's formula gives
$$
[x^{n}]\,T=\frac{1}{n}[u^{n-1}]\,\varphi(u)^{n}=\frac{1}{n}[u^{n-1}]\,e^{nu}=\frac{1}{n}\cdot\frac{n^{n-1}}{(n-1)!}=\frac{n^{n-1}}{n!},
$$
which agrees with the coefficients of $T$. $\checkmark$

## Step 2. Radius of convergence and boundary behavior

Differentiating (1): $T'=e^{T}+x\,e^{T}T'$, so using $xe^{T}=T$,
$$
T'=\frac{e^{T}}{1-T}.
$$
This diverges when $T\to 1$, which from (1) occurs at $x=T/e^{T}=1/e$. Hence the radius of convergence is $R=1/e$, and $x=1/e$ is the boundary point.

At $x=1/e$, the $n$-th term is, by Stirling's formula $n!\sim n^{n}e^{-n}\sqrt{2\pi n}$,
$$
\frac{e^{-n}\,n^{n-1}}{n!}\sim\frac{e^{-n}\,n^{n-1}}{n^{n}e^{-n}\sqrt{2\pi n}}=\frac{1}{n\sqrt{2\pi n}}\sim C\,n^{-3/2},
$$
which is summable. So the series converges at $x=1/e$, and by Abel's theorem the value $T(1/e)$ equals the limit of $T(x)$ as $x\to(1/e)^{-}$, which is continuous up to the boundary.

## Step 3. Evaluating at $x=1/e$

Setting $x=1/e$ in (1):
$$
T=\frac{1}{e}\,e^{T}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad T\,e^{-T}=e^{-1}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad (-T)\,e^{-T}=-e^{-1}.
$$
Recall the Lambert $W$ function, defined by $W(z)\,e^{W(z)}=z$. Thus $-T=W(-e^{-1})$.

The point $z=-1/e$ is the branch point of $W$, where the two real branches meet, and
$$
W_{0}(-1/e)=W_{-1}(-1/e)=-1.
$$
(Indeed $(-1)\cdot e^{-1}=-1/e$.) Therefore $-T=-1$, i.e.
$$
T(1/e)=1.
$$

## Conclusion

$$
\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\frac{e^{-j}\,j^{j-1}}{j!}=T(1/e)=1.
$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
